facts.text: Rehovot was founded in 1890 by Polish Jews of the First Aliyah, choosing a site near Khirbat Deiran to avoid Rothschild influence.
The city’s name means “wide expanse” in Hebrew, reflecting its early citrus orchards that stretched across the coastal plain.
In 1934, chemist Chaim Weizmann established a research institute that later became the Weizmann Institute of Science, Israel’s premier research university.
The 1920 opening of Rehovot Railway Station linked the town’s citrus trade to Tel Aviv and Jaffa, boosting export to Europe.
In 1987, authorities restored the former juice factory building and converted it into a historical museum, preserving industrial heritage.
Rehovot’s citrus industry once made it a self‑sufficient town, with the first orchard planted by Swiss descendant Zalma Minkov’s husband.
